reference.question: A triangle has vertices \(A(0,0)\), \(B(4,0)\), and \(C(0,3)\). What is the length of side \(AC\)?
reference.solution:
Method 1: Length as vector magnitude

The vector \(\overrightarrow{AC}=(0,3)\) has magnitude \(\sqrt{0+9}=3\).

Method 2: Distance along the y-axis

Both points lie on the \(y\)-axis, so their distance is the absolute difference of their \(y\)-coordinates: \(AC=|3-0|=3\).

edges.reason: Perpendicular constructions and uniqueness explain orthogonal projections, but plotting on an existing square grid needs only its given axes. Keep the useful geometry preparation without imposing the full construction workflow.
Each coordinate axis is a number line with an origin, a direction and a unit. Plotting and reading coordinates is impossible without understanding those three elements of a number line.
edges.scope: coordinate axes as two perpendicular number lines

edges.reason: Each axis is a signed number line, so plotting signed coordinates uses number-to-position interpretation on it.
edges.scope: axes as number lines with negatives

edges.reason: A point's two coordinates form an ordered pair; swapping the entries generally changes the point.
Quadrant signs and axis-coordinate restrictions refer to the coordinate plane's axes and ordered coordinates.
edges.scope: quadrant signs and points on axes

edges.reason: Absolute difference is one valid length formula. Sorting the coordinates and subtracting the smaller from the larger, or counting grid units, meets the actual criterion without evaluating absolute-value expressions.
edges.scope: Using the absolute coordinate-difference formula for an axis-parallel segment length

edges.reason: Gemini uses quadrant/axis features to assign coordinates in one diagram method. Coordinate differences and area can instead be computed from already supplied points without quadrant classification, so these features prepare rather than universally precede the task.
edges.scope: segment lengths and areas from coordinates

edges.reason: Endpoint displacements use Cartesian point coordinates.
edges.scope: computing coordinates from start and end point coordinates
